entries.appliesTo: persons who possess, distribute, or produce AI-generated (apparent) or obscene child sexual abuse material

sources.prohibition: 76-5b-207(2) — 'An actor commits possession of apparent child sexual abuse material if the actor intentionally or knowingly possesses, views, accesses with intent to view, or maintains access with intent to view apparent child sexual abuse material.'; 76-5b-103(1) — '"Apparent child sexual abuse material" means a visual depiction, generated or created through the use of artificial intelligence or generative artificial intelligence, or any other means, of a minor engaging in, observing, or being used for sexually explicit conduct'
sources.coveredSubjects: 76-5b-103(1) — 'of a minor engaging in, observing, or being used for sexually explicit conduct'; 76-5b-103(12) — '"Minor" means an individual who is younger than 18 years old.'
sources.enforcer: 67-5-21(1) — 'There is created within the Office of the Attorney General the Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) unit to investigate and prosecute cases involving child sexual abuse material, apparent child sexual abuse material, or obscene child sexual abuse material'

flags: Criminal tiers, no stated fines (rule 11): possession of apparent CSAM is 'a second degree felony' (76-5b-207(3)); distribution or production of apparent CSAM is 'a first degree felony', or 'a second degree felony' if the actor is under 18 (76-5b-208(3)); unlawful activity regarding obscene CSAM is 'a second degree felony' (76-5b-209(3)). No fine amounts appear in the bill, so no penaltyMax is coded.
Stacking: 'It is a separate offense... for each minor depicted... and for each time the same minor is depicted in different apparent child sexual abuse material' (76-5b-207(4), 76-5b-208(4)).
No real-victim element: 'proof that the minor depicted in the apparent child sexual abuse material is a real minor that exists is not required' (76-5b-207(6), 76-5b-208(5)).

The bill narrows the existing 'child sexual abuse material' definition by striking '[artificially generated and depicts an individual with substantial characteristics of a minor...]' (76-5b-103(3)) and moves AI-generated material into the standalone 'apparent child sexual abuse material' offenses.

New offenses are added to the sex-offender registry as registrable offenses with 10-year registration and removal-petition eligibility (53-29-202(1)(a)(xxvi)-(xxviii), 53-29-203, 53-29-205), and to habitual/repeat-offender enhancements (76-3-203.5, 76-3-407) and the RICO 'unlawful activity' list (76-17-401(4)(aa)-(cc)).

Conforming amendment extends the pre-existing computer-technician failure-to-report offense (class B misdemeanor) to apparent and obscene CSAM (76-5b-206) — a criminal reporting duty on individual technicians, not an ongoing company compliance duty; ISPs/interactive computer services are exempt if they report under 18 U.S.C. 2258A (76-5b-206(8)).

Safe harbor: entities and employees are not criminally or civilly liable for good-faith 'reporting or data preservation duties required under federal or state law' or 'implementing a policy of attempting to prevent the presence of apparent child sexual abuse material' (76-5b-207(7), 76-5b-208(6), 76-5b-209(5)).

Non-criminal conforming provisions: public-library state-funding filter condition extended to the new material categories (9-7-215(2)), DHHS material-handling rules (26B-1-234), background-check disqualifying offenses (26B-2-120, 81-9-402, 81-13-203), GRAMA records exclusion (63G-2-103(25)(b)), juvenile disposition guidelines (63M-7-404.5), forfeiture contraband definition (77-11a-101) — all reference the new definitions; no new company or education regime is created.
Effective date: 'This bill takes effect on May 6, 2026.' (Section 26)
